title: Group Theory Heist
subtitle: Which cricket team is manipulating their stats?
conceptSummary: GROUP BY groups rows with the same value, then aggregates each group. Perfect for 'total by category' questions.

dialogue.text: The cricket board suspects match-fixing is inflating team scores. We need total runs PER TEAM.
GROUP BY team_id with SUM(runs_scored). One row per team. That's the pattern.

teachMoment.title: GROUP BY: One Row Per Group
teachMoment.body:
GROUP BY groups identical values and lets you aggregate each group:

SELECT team_id, SUM(runs_scored) AS total_runs
FROM match_stats
GROUP BY team_id

Result: one row per team, showing their total runs. Without GROUP BY, SUM would give ONE total for ALL teams.

task.instruction: Find the total runs scored by each player (player_id). Show player_id and total_runs. Sort by total_runs descending.
task.startingQuery:
SELECT player_id, SUM(runs_scored) AS total_runs
FROM match_stats
GROUP BY 
ORDER BY total_runs DESC
task.solution: SELECT player_id, SUM(runs_scored) AS total_runs FROM match_stats GROUP BY player_id ORDER BY total_runs DESC

hints.text: GROUP BY goes after FROM (and WHERE if you have one). What column are you grouping by?
GROUP BY player_id — this groups all stat rows for the same player together.
SELECT player_id, SUM(runs_scored) AS total_runs FROM match_stats GROUP BY player_id ORDER BY total_runs DESC

winDialogue.text: Player 1 has 202 total runs, far ahead of everyone else. That's a statistical anomaly!
We need to filter groups — find only players with suspiciously high runs. HAVING is the tool for that.

storyBeat: Player 1 (Arjun Patel) has double the runs of any other player. The data manipulation is clear. Now we need to isolate ALL anomalies — players with more than 100 total runs.
